newsitem.title: USA: U.S. positive on N. Korea food appeal - officials.
newsitem.headline: U.S. positive on N. Korea food appeal - officials.

text.p: The World Food Programme is expected to make a formal appeal for new food aid for North Korea in the next week and the United States is likely to respond positively, U.S. officials said on Thursday.

The comments by State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns appeared designed to reassure Pyongyang that Washington sympathised with its food problems and to resolve a disagreement that has kept North Korea from attending an important briefing on Korean peninsula peace talks.
"I think there's going to be an appeal for food by the World Food Programme ... It's considering a formal appeal during the next week, similar to one issued last year," Burns told reporters.
He said the United States would look at such an appeal "very carefully, consult with South Korea, with our allies and decide on an appropriate response."
"I would remind you that we have responded positively to every previous appeal by the World Food Programme in the last year or two," he said.

"We believe there is a serious food problem in North Korea and we're sympathetic to the plight of the North Korean people and we encourage private assistance to the North Koreans ... They are desperate for food and they've made an official appeal and now the U.N.'s responding," he added.
It was the second straight day that Burns had sent a strong signal to Pyongyang that additional U.S. food aid may soon be made available.
"I wanted to reinforce what I said yesterday," he said of the reason for going out of his way to repeat his earlier comments.
It could not immediately be determined how large the World Food Programme appeal would be and how much the United States would contribute. Last year, Washington gave $8.2 million.

North Korea's ambassador to the United Nations, in an interview with CNN on Tuesday, said that a briefing on the U.S.-South Korean proposal for Korean peninsula peace talks was twice delayed because Washington had not carried through on its promise to provide the food aid.

The United States insists it never promised Pyongyang a specific amount of food aid in return for North Korea's participation in the briefing, which is intended to bring North and South into a dialogue that will defuse tensions -- and eventually bring about a permanent peace -- on the Korean peninsula which was divided in the 1950-53 Korean War.
But Washington did approve an application for a private American grain company, Minneapolis-based Cargill Inc., for a license to export grain to North Korea.
Those negotiations have bogged down over financing for the deal and the adminstration has refused to become involved in what it has called "commercial transactions" between North Korea and Cargill.
But U.S. officials, in signalling a willingness to respond positively to the World Food Programme appeal, have shown an eagerness to provide food aid over which it has control.
North Korea has tried to pressure the United States to help finance the grain deal, hoping Washington might be more willing to help if it meant the diplomatic talks would proceed.
But Burns has said no further dates will be set for the talks until the U.S. side is confident that the North Koreans will actually attend the meetings.
